x.ASV: For the Chief Musician; on stringed instruments. A Psalm of David. Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness; Thou hast set me at large when I was in distress: Have mercy upon me, and hear my prayer.
x.Darby: To the chief Musician. On stringed instruments. A Psalm of David. When I call, answer me, OGod of my righteousness: in pressure thou hast enlarged me; be gracious unto me, and hear my prayer.
x.KJV: To the chief Musician on Neginoth, A Psalm of David. Hear me when I call, O God of my righteousness: thou hast enlarged me when I was in distress; have mercy upon me, and hear my prayer.
x.YLT: To the Overseer with Stringed Instruments. --A Psalm of David. In my calling answer Thou me, O God of my righteousness. In adversity Thou gavest enlargement to me; Favour me, and hear my prayer.

nt: Here **God of my righteousness** could mean: (1) my righteous God or (2) God who vindicates me. Both options are grammatically possible, and both fit the context well. The following relative clause (verse 1b), which highlights God’s past faithfulness, may suggest that it is God’s righteousness that is in view (hence the UST rendering). You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my God, the righteous one]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **distress**, you could express the same idea in another way. The original word is related to narrowness. Alternate translation: [in trouble] or [when I am oppressed]

x.ASV: O ye sons of men, how long shall my glory be turned into dishonor? How long will ye love vanity, and seek after falsehood? [Selah
x.Darby: Ye sons of men, till when is my glory [to be put] to shame? [How long] will ye love vanity, will ye seek after a lie? Selah.
x.KJV: O ye sons of men, how long will ye turn my glory into shame? how long will ye love vanity, and seek after leasing? Selah.
x.YLT: Sons of men! till when is my glory for shame? Ye love a vain thing, ye seek a lie. Selah.

nt: **Son of man** could refer to: (1) the mortality and finitude of his enemies (as opposed to God’s eternal infinitude), (2) important or wealthy men, or (3) the fact that the psalmist is now addressing people rather than God. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [You men]
עַד־מֶ֬ה כְבוֹדִ֣⁠י לִ֭⁠כְלִמָּה תֶּאֱהָב֣וּ⁠ן רִ֑יק תְּבַקְשׁ֖וּ כָזָ֣ב

The psalmist is using the question form to rebuke his enemies. If you would not use the question form for this purpose in your language, you could translate these three questions as statements or exclamations. Alternate translation: [stop calling glory shame! Stop loving futility! Stop seeking falsehood!]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **glory** and **shame**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [you consider my glorious deeds as shameful deeds]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **futility** and **falsehood**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [How long will you love vain things? How long will you pursue untrue things?]

x.ASV: But know that Jehovah hath set apart for himself him that is godly: Jehovah will hear when I call unto him.
x.Darby: But know that Jehovah hath set apart the pious [man] for himself: Jehovah will hear when I call unto him.
x.KJV: But know that the Lord hath set apart him that is godly for himself: the Lord will hear when I call unto him.
x.YLT: And know ye that Jehovah Hath separated a saintly one to Himself. Jehovah heareth in my calling to Him.

nt: David is using the adjective **godly** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [godly people]

x.ASV: Stand in awe, and sin not: Commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. [Selah
x.Darby: Be moved with anger, and sin not; meditate in your own hearts upon your bed, and be still. Selah.
x.KJV: Stand in awe, and sin not: commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still. Selah.
x.YLT: `Tremble ye, and do not sin;' Say ye thus in your heart on your bed, And be ye silent. Selah.

nt: The implication could be: (1) that the hearers should **tremble** in fear of Yahweh’s punishment for the unfaithful or (2) that if the hearers are angry, they should control themselves and not sin. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Tremble in fear and do not sin] or [Even if you tremble in anger, do not sin]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and motives exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Consider your thoughts and motives]

The Hebrew root words for speak, **heart**, and **bed** in this verse appear in verses 6 (as “say”), 7, and 8 (as “lie down”) respectively (in the same order). Consider if a similar pattern would create a natural poetic effect in your language.

Here, **be silent** means that the listeners should show self-control and not act on sinful impulses. You could include this information in your translation if it would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and do not act on evil thoughts]

x.ASV: Offer the sacrifices of righteousness, And put your trust in Jehovah.
x.Darby: Offer sacrifices of righteousness, and confide in Jehovah.
x.KJV: Offer the sacrifices of righteousness, and put your trust in the Lord.
x.YLT: Sacrifice ye sacrifices of righteousness, And trust ye unto Jehovah.

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [sacrifices that are righteous]

The words **righteousness** and **trust** form the poetic center of this psalm. **Righteousness** is mentioned in [verse 1](../004/001.md) and **trust** is the same word translated as “securely” in [verse 8](../004/008.md). You may wish to explore whether you can reflect this symmetry in a natural way in your language.

x.ASV: Many there are that say, Who will show us any good? Jehovah, lift thou up the light of thy countenance upon us.
x.Darby: Many say, Who shall cause us to see good? Lift up upon us the light of thy countenance, O Jehovah.
x.KJV: There be many that say, Who will shew us any good? Lord, lift thou up the light of thy countenance upon us.
x.YLT: Many are saying, `Who doth show us good?' Lift on us the light of Thy face, O Jehovah,

nt: The people asking this are using the question form to make a complaint and an implied request. If you would not use the question form for this purpose in your language, you could translate this as an exclamation or plain request. Alternate translation: [No one is showing us good!] or [Please, someone show us good!]

Here, **good** is spoken of as if it were something that someone could **show** to someone else. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Who will do good things for us]

The writer speaks of Yahweh acting favorably towards them as if Yahweh’s face shone a light on them. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Act favorably towards us]
This is a reference to the high priest’s blessing in [Numbers 6:25](../../num/06/25.md).

x.ASV: Thou hast put gladness in my heart, More than they have when their grain and their new wine are increased.
x.Darby: Thou hast put joy in my heart, more than in the time that their corn and their new wine was in abundance.
x.KJV: Thou hast put gladness in my heart, more than in the time that their corn and their wine increased.
x.YLT: Thou hast given joy in my heart, From the time their corn and their wine Have been multiplied.

nt: Here the phrase **put joy in my heart** represents that the author’s emotional state is joyful. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You have made me happy]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [You have made me glad]

Here, **grain and new wine** represent basic food necessities. An abundance of them represents material prosperity. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have a lot of bread and fresh milk] or [they are quite rich]
In Hebrew, this verse uses progressively shorter lines and repeated sounds to create a sense of peaceful rest. Consider if there is a way in your language to create the same sensation.

x.ASV: In peace will I both lay me down and sleep; For thou, Jehovah, alone makest me dwell in safety.
x.Darby: In peace will I both lay me down and sleep; for thou, Jehovah, alone makest me to dwell in safety.
x.KJV: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, Lord, only makest me dwell in safety.
x.YLT: In peace together I lie down and sleep, For Thou, O Jehovah, alone, In confidence dost cause me to dwell!

nt: בְּ⁠שָׁל֣וֹם יַחְדָּו֮ אֶשְׁכְּבָ֪ה וְ⁠אִ֫ישָׁ֥ן כִּֽי־אַתָּ֣ה יְהוָ֣ה לְ⁠בָדָ֑ד לָ֝⁠בֶ֗טַח תּוֹשִׁיבֵֽ⁠נִי

If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since you alone, Yahweh, cause me to dwell securely, therefore in peace I will both lie down and sleep.]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Peacefully]
